translations.0: Why is being resilient connected with bouncing back?
translations.1: Elastic; able to recover from difficulty.
translations.2: The key is recovery after being affected, not never being affected.
translations.3: The Latin source of resilient is connected with jumping or springing back. Picture a branch that returns to its shape after being bent.
translations.4: The word first concerned returning to a position, then materials recovering after pressure, and later people recovering from difficulty. The metaphor does not mean a person never feels hurt or sad.
translations.7: See how the adjective becomes a noun meaning resilience.
translations.9: Compare being strong with being able to recover.
translations.12: Being able to recover after being affected.
translations.13: Bouncing back emphasizes recovery, rather than never being affected.
translations.14: Why is resilience more than merely enduring?
translations.15: Resilience; the capacity to recover or spring back.
translations.16: Use the image of springing back to connect material elasticity with human recovery.
translations.17: Resilience is historically connected with Latin resilire, meaning to spring back; re- contributes the idea of returning.
translations.18: Think of resilience as the name of an ability. Use the adjective resilient to describe a person or material with that ability.
translations.20: Switch to the adjective and see how it describes people and materials.
translations.21: Which word names the capacity to recover?
translations.22: Resilience is a noun; resilient is an adjective.
translations.23: Why is the word for an asset connected with enough?
translations.24: An asset; a valuable person or thing.
translations.25: Understand assets through the idea of property sufficient to pay obligations.
translations.26: Assets is connected with Old French assez, meaning enough. Early legal uses concerned property sufficient to meet debts and other obligations, later developing into property and assets more generally.
translations.27: The singular asset was later formed from assets. It can also mean a useful person or advantage, such as valuable experience.
translations.30: Another business word, not a shared root: explore a different history of equity.
translations.31: Compare the contexts in which assets and capital are used.
translations.32: What does asset mean in Her experience is an asset?
translations.33: Money she has in a bank account.
translations.35: An asset can be a useful ability or advantage, not only financial property.
translations.36: Why can equity mean both fairness and an ownership interest?
translations.37: Fairness; equity in law; an ownership or financial interest.
translations.38: A useful connection is the idea of rights that someone ought fairly to enjoy.
translations.39: Equity can be traced through French to Latin forms associated with equality and fairness. Equitable principles in law are an important branch of its meaning.
translations.40: It also came to describe rights that someone properly holds. In finance, equity and equities concern ownership interests and shares. Context matters: equity does not always mean shares.
translations.43: Trace the shared linguistic idea of equality and fairness.
translations.44: Compare equity with assets in business contexts; they are not synonyms.
translations.45: How should equity in education be understood?
translations.46: Ownership of shares in education businesses.
translations.48: The context is education, so equity means fairness rather than company shares.
translations.49: How did writing underneath become underwriting insurance or securities?
translations.50: To underwrite insurance or securities; to provide financial support.
translations.51: Remember accepting responsibility through the image of signing underneath a document.
translations.52: Underwrite was connected with writing beneath a document and signing agreement. This literal image helps connect the word with its insurance meaning.
translations.53: Signing a marine insurance document came to signify accepting responsibility for an agreed loss. Underwrite developed insurance and financial-guarantee senses, and is also used for securities underwriting. The intended sense depends on context.
translations.56: See what the person or organization performing this role is called.
translations.58: Another word connected with writing one's name underneath.
translations.59: What does signing underneath mainly represent in this history?
translations.60: Agreeing and accepting the corresponding responsibility.
translations.61: Erasing the bottom of a document.
translations.62: Signing became associated with agreement and responsibility, leading to later insurance uses.
translations.63: Is mort in mortgage really connected with death?
translations.64: A mortgage loan; to secure a loan against real property.
translations.65: Its older form literally suggests a dead pledge, not having to repay for the rest of one's life.
translations.66: Mortgage comes from Old French mort, dead, and gage, a pledge or security. These are its historical components.
translations.67: A traditional explanation is that repayment or default brings the pledge arrangement to an end. Think of the end of the security arrangement, not the borrower's lifespan.
translations.69: A mortgage and a general loan do not have exactly the same scope.
translations.70: Move from borrowing to bearing risk: this is a topic connection, not a shared root.
translations.71: Which claim cannot be inferred from this etymology of mortgage?
translations.73: The loan must be repaid until the borrower dies.
translations.74: Dead describes the pledge in the older expression, not the borrower's lifespan.
translations.75: Why does the history of company involve bread?
translations.76: A company; a group of people; companionship.
translations.77: Connect people sharing bread with companions, groups, and working together.
translations.78: Company came through Old French. Its earlier Latin source combines ideas of together and bread, referring to people sharing a meal.
translations.79: From companions and people acting together to a business group, companionship and a company become connected meanings. This does not imply that modern companies originally sold bread.
translations.81: Another word connected with companionship and sharing.
translations.82: From a company to capital: a thematic rather than a root connection.
translations.83: What does company mean in I enjoy your company?
translations.86: Company also means companionship; the sentence is not discussing a business.
translations.87: Why can capital mean a chief city, a large letter, and business wealth?
translations.88: A capital city; capital funds; an uppercase letter; principal.
translations.89: Head and chief provide a memory connection between these branches.
translations.90: Capital is connected with Latin caput, head, and developed ideas of being chief or principal. Capital letters occur at the starts of sentences or names; a capital city is the main seat of government.
translations.91: The financial sense developed through principal property, the principal sum, and wealth used in business. The meanings arose along related historical branches, rather than from a single mechanical formula.
translations.93: From capital to people or systems associated with it.
translations.94: Compare capital and assets without treating them as synonyms.
translations.98: This is a writing context, not a financial one.
translations.99: How can a concession be both a compromise and a special right?
translations.100: Think of yielding or allowing in two different contexts.
translations.101: In negotiation, a concession is something one side gives up. In business, it may be a granted operating right. Both connect with giving, allowing, or yielding.
translations.102: Con- in this word should not mechanically be read as together. The historical material below follows concession itself rather than repeating a whole root family's story.
translations.105: Return to the verb and understand the act of acknowledging or yielding.
translations.107: Follow the ced/cess connection and see how retreating enters economic language.
translations.108: What does make a concession usually mean in negotiations?
translations.109: Make a compromise or yield a point.
translations.111: It means yielding a condition or position, not setting out or travelling.
translations.112: What is the difference between process and procedure?
translations.113: How something unfolds is not the same as the prescribed steps for doing it.
translations.114: Procedure is historically connected with going forward. In modern usage, focus on a method, set of steps, or formalities for handling a matter.
translations.115: Process can emphasize how an activity or change unfolds; procedure often means a prescribed sequence of steps. A shared ced/cess connection does not make them interchangeable.
translations.118: One emphasizes a process; the other often emphasizes prescribed steps.
translations.120: See how to express continuing or proceeding.
translations.123: A set of safety steps to follow.
translations.124: Procedure here means an operating procedure that must be followed.
translations.125: Success, successful, or successfully: which belongs in the sentence?
translations.126: Their meanings connect, but one is a noun, one an adjective, and one an adverb.
translations.127: Successful combines success with -ful to describe something effective or successful. Adding -ly gives successfully, which modifies an action.
translations.128: First decide whether you are describing a quality or how an action was completed, then choose the form.
translations.131: Return to the noun and see success used as a concept.
translations.132: Move from adjective to adverb for a more precise sentence.
translations.133: Which form completes The project was _____?
translations.134: An adjective is needed here to describe the project's state.
translations.135: Why can photograph be remembered as recording with light?
translations.136: Photo- relates to light, while -graph relates to recording or drawing.
translations.137: Photograph provides a clear word-formation example: light helps create an image, and recording or depicting is the result. Combining the parts gives a memorable picture.
translations.138: Continue to photographer and photographic, noticing how suffixes turn a photograph into a person who photographs or an adjective about photography.
translations.140: -er points to the person who does the photography.
translations.141: Notice how an adjective describes techniques or works.
translations.142: What does photo- chiefly suggest in photograph?
translations.145: Photo- is associated with light; tele- commonly supplies the idea of distance.
translations.146: How is sound from far away built into telephone?
translations.147: Tele- contributes distance and -phone contributes sound.
translations.148: Telephone combines distance and sound, expressing the purpose of transmitting sound over a distance.
translations.149: Now compare microphone: the ending still relates to sound, but the beginning changes. Comparing the parts offers more than memorizing one translation.
translations.152: They share a sound-related element but use different prefixes.
translations.154: Move from a device to speech sounds themselves.
translations.155: What does tele- relate to in telephone?
translations.158: It contributes the idea of distance; the other element supplies sound.
translations.159: How do bio- and -logy form the name of a subject?
translations.160: Connect life with study so that biology becomes more than a string of letters.
translations.161: As a learning analysis of the modern word, bio- suggests life and -logy commonly appears in names of fields of study.
translations.162: This helps explain word formation; it does not mean every word ending in -logy has exactly the same kind of study meaning. Compare biological to see how the ending changes word class.
translations.164: From a subject's name to an adjective meaning biological.
translations.165: It also concerns life, but -graphy points to writing or recording rather than the same academic subject.
translations.166: What does bio- suggest in biology?
translations.169: Bio- is commonly associated with life.
translations.170: How does forming again help us understand reform?
translations.171: Re- and form are a starting point, but reform does not mean simply repeating old practices.
translations.172: Reform is connected with Latin, French, and English forms meaning to form again or reshape. It can be a noun or a verb in modern English.
translations.173: In institutional and procedural contexts, it often means improving or changing a system. Roots provide a clue, while the sentence determines the intended meaning.
translations.175: Both contain form, but their prefixes give different emphases.
translations.176: Return to the act or result of forming.
translations.177: What does reform usually mean in an institutional context?
